questions.question: Chart, values, release — which mapping is correct?
options: Chart=package of templates, values=configuration injected into them, release=a named installed instance
questions.explanation: The chart is the reusable package; values parameterize it; a release is one installation of that chart with those values, tracked with revisions in the cluster.

questions.question: In Chart.yaml, what's the difference between `version` and `appVersion`?
options: version is the chart package's semver; appVersion records the application version it deploys by default
appVersion is the Kubernetes API version
questions.explanation: The chart itself evolves independently of the app it packages: fixing a template bug bumps version, shipping app 2.3.0 bumps appVersion (often used as the default image tag).

questions.question: What is the values precedence, lowest to highest?
options: All are merged with equal priority
questions.explanation: Chart defaults are the base; each -f file overlays them in order; --set flags override everything. That's why env files hold the real config and --set is reserved for one-off overrides like image tags in CI.

questions.question: Which command renders a chart's manifests locally WITHOUT touching a cluster?
questions.explanation: helm template runs the template engine client-side and prints the YAML — ideal for CI validation, debugging template logic, and feeding GitOps tools. (install --dry-run also renders but contacts the cluster for validation.)

questions.question: Why is `helm upgrade --install` the standard deploy command in CI pipelines?
options: It skips hooks, making deploys faster
It's idempotent: installs the release if absent, upgrades it if present — one command for first and every subsequent deploy
questions.explanation: Pipelines shouldn't need if-first-time logic. upgrade --install (often with --atomic --wait) converges to the desired release state whether or not it already exists.

questions.question: What does the --atomic flag on helm upgrade do?
options: Runs the upgrade in a single API call
Automatically rolls back to the previous revision if the upgrade fails (waiting for resources to be ready)
Locks the release against concurrent upgrades only
questions.explanation: --atomic implies --wait: Helm waits for resources to become ready and, on timeout/failure, restores the previous revision — turning a bad deploy into a no-op instead of an outage.

questions.question: helm rollback can restore a release to any previous revision recorded in its history.
questions.explanation: True. Each install/upgrade stores a revision (in Secrets by default); `helm history <release>` lists them and `helm rollback <release> <rev>` re-applies that revision's manifests.

questions.question: Uninstalling a Helm release always deletes the PersistentVolumeClaims created while it ran.
questions.explanation: False. Many charts (databases especially) create PVCs via StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates, which survive uninstall to protect data. Reinstalling can then reuse old credentials/data — clean them explicitly when you truly want a fresh start.

questions.question: You change a value that only affects a ConfigMap, but pods keep running with old config. What's the established chart pattern to force a rolling restart on config changes?
options: Set replicas to 0 and back in two upgrades
Add a checksum/config annotation on the pod template that hashes the rendered ConfigMap
questions.explanation: Hashing the config into a pod-template annotation means any config change alters the template, so the Deployment performs a rolling update. Without it, env-var consumers never see the new values.

questions.question: One chart must serve dev (1 replica, no TLS) and prod (5 replicas, TLS ingress). What's the idiomatic structure?
options: Two divergent copies of the chart
Single chart with feature flags in templates; per-environment values files (values-dev.yaml, values-prod.yaml)
Hardcode prod settings; patch dev with kubectl edit
questions.explanation: The chart encodes ALL capabilities behind values (`{{- if .Values.ingress.enabled }}`); environments differ only by values file. Duplicate charts drift apart within weeks — the values-file diff IS your environment documentation.

questions.question: Write the command to list Helm releases across ALL namespaces.
questions.explanation: helm list is namespace-scoped by default; -A/--all-namespaces surveys the whole cluster — first command when auditing what's installed where.

questions.question: Write the command to roll back release `api` to revision 3 in namespace `prod`.
questions.explanation: helm rollback <release> <revision> with the namespace flag. Check `helm history api -n prod` first to pick the right revision.

questions.question: In a template, what does `{{ .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion }}` do?
options: Throws an error if image.tag is unset
Uses image.tag from values if set, otherwise falls back to the chart's appVersion
questions.explanation: Pipelines pass the left value through the function: default returns the fallback only when the input is empty. This is the standard pattern letting CI override the tag while keeping a sane default.

questions.question: Where does Helm 3 store release state?
options: As Secrets (by default) in the release's namespace
questions.explanation: Helm 3 removed Tiller; release metadata lives in Kubernetes Secrets (sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<rev>) in the release namespace, secured by ordinary RBAC. Client-side config is just repos and cache.
